DELIVERY & ENGINEERING / 01

Faster code.
Better delivery?

The case for redesigning software delivery around AI—and using specifications to keep it connected to business intent.

Shervin Sadeghi · Scope AI · 30 October 2026

IN THIS ARTICLE

The delivery bottleneckThe delegation balanceWhy specifications helpAcross the lifecycleMeasure the whole outcomeSources & perspective

AI can produce a first implementation quickly. The business still needs the right software, reviewed, tested and ready to operate. Scope AI’s position is to redesign that whole journey around human judgement and meaningful AI assistance.

Improve the flow of delivery.

If coding becomes faster while requirements, review, testing and release remain constrained, work can accumulate in a different queue. More generated code may increase the amount waiting for validation.

AN ILLUSTRATION, NOT A BENCHMARK

If coding takes 30 of 100 units of sequential delivery time, making coding three times faster reduces the total to 80 units: a 20% reduction, before any additional rework.

Real delivery includes parallel work and dependencies, so the calculation is deliberately simple. The lesson is to measure the whole process and find its constraints. Models and tools matter; the workflow determines how effectively their capabilities become useful outcomes.

Find the right level of delegation.

Too little

People do all the analysis, design and planning. AI is asked to write an isolated function. Much of the intellectual effort remains unchanged.

Too much

“Build an e-commerce shop” leaves payment rules, inventory behaviour and access decisions implicit. Assumptions can spread through a large implementation.

Within clear boundaries

AI asks questions, drafts requirements, compares options and implements bounded changes. People own consequential decisions and acceptance.

The human role expands toward framing, directing and validating work. That requires enough technical and business understanding to challenge what AI produces.

A fast first draft can become a long correction loop.

With loosely directed vibe coding, the pattern can become: prompt, generate code, discover a mismatch, prompt again, regenerate and review again. Each correction may disturb behaviour that was already right, while the intended outcome stays scattered across messages.

A reviewed specification makes expected behaviour, constraints, exceptions and acceptance examples available before consequential implementation. AI can help create it by synthesizing evidence and exposing unanswered questions. It becomes a shared agreement for implementation and testing.

This is a hypothesis about reducing avoidable rework, not a claim that specifications eliminate iteration. Prototypes are useful for discovering needs. Capture that learning, inspect retained code and keep the specification current as decisions change.

Spec-driven development can be lightweight and iterative. A small, understood change may need only a short task contract. A change affecting financial calculations or access rights needs more explicit treatment.

Give AI meaningful work across the lifecycle.

IBM’s overview describes AI assistance spanning requirements, design, coding, testing, deployment and operational feedback. Scope AI proposes connecting those activities through reviewed context, bounded authority and acceptance evidence.

  1. Discover and specify. Synthesize approved interviews, emails, surveys and tickets into evidence-linked findings and candidate user stories. Flag contradictions instead of inventing answers.
  2. Design and implement. Compare design options, explain existing code and implement small changes against accepted requirements. Existing behaviour is evidence of what code does, not proof of what it should do.
  3. Verify and release. Derive tests from stories and acceptance criteria. Prepare infrastructure as code and deployment evidence within explicit permissions. People review consequential decisions and authorize release.
  4. Learn and improve. Analyze logs, defects and feedback. Distinguish a defect against an existing requirement from a new need before proposing the next increment.

These are responsibilities, not a requirement for a separate agent at every step. A coding agent is one specialized form of AI agent. Using AI to build software is also distinct from building an application that contains AI.

ILLUSTRATIVE ONBOARDING EXAMPLE

Repeated status enquiries suggest that applicants cannot see what happens after submission. AI can group the evidence and propose a progress-visibility story. A business owner decides which statuses are visible, what “current” means and what happens on failure. Those decisions guide code and tests; later feedback shows whether the problem was solved.

Measure accepted outcomes.

Faster generation creates value only when it improves the overall result. Start with one bounded pilot and compare end-to-end lead time, total human effort, review delays, rework, escaped defects and total cost against a credible baseline.

Include the time spent preparing specifications and reviewing generated work. Keep increments small enough to examine. Tests must challenge assumptions: passing a test based on an invented rule does not establish business correctness.

Scope AI is developing this approach for knowledge-intensive delivery, informed by financial-services business analysis and validation experience. Its benefits must be demonstrated through measured work; no specific productivity gain is promised.
